Fascinating Baby Bump Facts That Will Change How You Look at Your Pregnant Body

by Marygrace Taylor
Medically Reviewed by Jennifer Wu, M.D., F.A.C.O.G.
Medical Review Policy
All What to Expect content that addresses health or safety is medically reviewed by a team of vetted health professionals. Our Medical Review Board includes OB/GYNs, pediatricians, infectious disease specialists, doulas, lactation counselors, endocrinologists, fertility specialists and more. 

We believe you should always know the source of the information you're reading. Learn more about our editorial and medical review policies.

Your baby bump is probably one of the most exciting parts of pregnancy. Here are 10 fun things you might not know about it.
Back to Top
In This Article
  • When will my bump be noticeable?
  • When do stretch marks show up?
  • When will I feel my baby move?
  • What's that dark line down the center of my belly?
  • Will my innie become an outie?
  • Can my baby hear my voice through my belly?
  • Does my baby know when I rub my belly?
  • Is it okay if my bump is measuring a little big or small?
  • Will my big belly make me uncomfortable?
  • Will my bump disappear after giving birth?

Instaread

Your beautiful baby bump is fun to show off, but it also reflects your changing pregnancy. The skin on your belly may change as it grows; you'll feel and see your baby's movements; and you'll even communicate with your baby via your bump.

From when it first appears to when it disappears — and everything in between — here are some questions you might have about your baby bump.

Key Takeaways
  • Your baby bump changes throughout pregnancy. From barely showing in the first trimester to developing stretch marks, a dark linea nigra, or a protruding belly button, most physical changes are normal and often fade after birth.
  • Your growing belly is a connection to your baby. As pregnancy progresses, your baby will be able to hear your voice and respond to your touch. In turn, you’ll feel (and see) your baby’s movements.
  • Your body continues to change until — and after — delivery. As your baby grows, discomforts like heartburn or round ligament pain may increase. Your postpartum belly will take time to recover as your uterus and abdominal muscles heal.

When will my bump be noticeable?

Despite how you're feeling on the inside, chances are your bump won't start to show until you hit the 3-month mark, when your baby is about the size of a lime. Before that, your baby is still tiny. Even at 4 weeks, she's only the size of a poppy seed!

"Something that helps me is monthly bump pics so I can compare what my belly looked like at 12 weeks and 16 weeks and how much my bump has grown," says What to Expect Community mom humanjukebox. "It's one of those things we see every day, so it's hard to see all the little changes adding up."

When do stretch marks show up?

If you're among the more than half of pregnant women who develop skin streaks, you'll start to notice them when you're between 13 weeks and 21 weeks.

These marks form when the supporting layers beneath your skin stretch as your belly grows. The streaks might become darker and more prominent when your tummy really starts to stretch around the 35-week mark.

There's no proven way to prevent stretch marks, and they usually fade after you give birth. But in the meantime, try to embrace them. Your body is growing to make a baby!

"I was bummed when I started seeing them at 36 weeks," says Community mom SierraRoseG. "I mentioned it to my husband and he said, 'I think they're pretty cool, they look like tiger stripes.' If you're gonna be stuck with them, learn to love them and accept that sometimes they're just part of the journey in getting your sweet bundle of joy."

Keep track of your pregnancy symptoms, get more expert advice, and connect with other moms who are due the same month in the free What to Expect app Opens a new window.

When will I feel my baby move?

If you feel a fluttering sensation, it could very well be your baby squirming or fidgeting. This early movement — called quickening — usually starts when you're around 4 or 5 months pregnant. Trusted SourceAmerican College of Obstetricians and GynecologistsHow Your Fetus Grows During PregnancySee All Sources [1]

Community mom Halesbbb says she felt that "first flutter at 13 weeks," while Community mom amjamc says she "felt fluttering movements at 19 weeks."

From then on, your baby will only get more active. By 6 months, you might start to feel tiny feet pitter-pattering. And by 28 weeks, your health care practitioner will want you to start "counting kicks," or fetal movements, to ensure your baby is doing well.

What's that dark line down the center of my belly?

The dark, vertical line extending from your belly button to your pubic area is your linea nigra, or bump line, and it usually becomes noticeable around 23 weeks.

Like other skin changes during pregnancy, the linea nigra is caused by surging pregnancy hormones. It's perfectly normal and will probably fade a few months after you give birth.

"Well even stranger is that I grew more fuzzy hairs on my belly, so though my line is only slightly noticeable, the hair does accentuate it," says Community mom MichMonja.

Will my innie become an outie?

If your belly button is an innie, it won't stay that way for long. Around 26 weeks, your expanding uterus will cause your belly button to protrude, making it look like an outie.

"I honestly think it looks so cute on a baby bump!" says Community mom Mads-.

Like most of the other changes happening to your body these days, this one is harmless — and things will go back to normal after you have the baby and your stomach deflates.

What if your belly button is pierced? As long as your belly button piercing is healed (as in, not freshly done) and healthy, there's no reason to remove your navel ring right now. Toward the end of pregnancy, you may want to switch to wearing a straight plastic bar, which may feel more comfortable and is safer than metal jewelry in the event you need an emergency C-section.

If at any point your stretching belly makes your piercing irritating, you might want to take it out. You should also remove it if the skin around the ring seems red or inflamed, which could be signs of infection.

Can my baby hear my voice through my belly?

By as early as 16 weeks, your baby's ears are developed enough that she can hear your voice. At that point, she's mostly just listening. But by 26 weeks, her brain is developed to the point where your baby can respond to stimuli. So don't be surprised if she gives a little kick when you talk or sing to her!

Speaking of songs, you might want to think about finding a special one to play for your baby. While there's no proof that playing certain music (like classical) will boost your baby's IQ, sharing your favorite tunes can still be a fun bonding experience. 

Of course, everything will sound a little muffled in there. To get an idea of what things sound like for your baby, try talking with your hand over your mouth. That's what your baby hears!

"During the last ultrasound when we needed her to move, I would speak to her and she would jump!" says Community mom Vendemiaire.

Does my baby know when I rub my belly?

Yes! Touching, patting, or holding your bump doesn't just make you feel warm and fuzzy, it might make your baby feel good, too. Research shows that babies in the womb respond to belly touches by moving around. Trusted SourcePLOS OneFetal Behavioural Responses to Maternal Voice and TouchSee All Sources [2] So keep rubbing that bump!

"Every time I touch my belly, my baby starts moving so intensely," says Community mom samileigh12. "He will even kick following my hand movements!"

Because touch can stimulate your baby, it can be especially helpful when you start counting kicks. And of course, it's an amazing way to bond.

Is it okay if my bump is measuring a little big or small?

A couple of centimeters big or small is nothing to worry about. At each prenatal visit, your practitioner uses a tape measure to check your fundal height — the distance from your pubic bone to the top of your uterus. That measurement in centimeters usually corresponds to how many weeks pregnant you are.

Often, measuring big or small during pregnancy could just mean that your due date is off by a few days or a week, or that your baby is sitting high in your uterus. It doesn't mean that your baby isn't growing fast enough or will be too big to deliver vaginally.

"I've measured two weeks ahead and the same day had a sono where the baby was perfectly average for growth" says Community mom bbgirl2020.

Will my big belly make me uncomfortable?

As your baby takes up more and more space in your belly — growing from about 2 pounds at the end of the second trimester to somewhere between 6 and 9 pounds at the end of the third trimester — you might start noticing some not-so-fun changes.

You might feel sharp pains as your round ligaments stretch to accommodate your growing bump. Heartburn could also become an issue, since your expanding uterus is now pushing on your stomach. 

"I'm 38 weeks tomorrow and the heaviness has fully kicked in," says Community mom anoncm, who suffers from round ligament pain. "I've been lying down as much as I can, but lying down also activates my heartburn."

Things are getting cramped for your baby, too, so don't be surprised if you notice fewer strong kicks and more stretches, rolls, and jabs from knees and elbows during the last few weeks of your pregnancy. Trusted SourceMayo ClinicFetal Development: The Third TrimesterSee All Sources [3] (Always check in with your practitioner about any changes in fetal movement, though.)

The good news is that the two of you are almost at the finish line. It won't be long now before you finally get to meet!

Will my bump disappear after giving birth?

Your bump won’t disappear right away. After you welcome your little one to the world, your postpartum recovery period begins. It takes some time for your uterus (and abdominal muscles and skin) to adapt, just like they did during pregnancy.

"My belly has finally gone down quite a bit," reports Community mom bigbobababy. "I started noticing a real improvement around 6 months postpartum. I honestly thought I'd be carting around a big belly forever."

If your belly still has a bump-like appearance several months after giving birth and you have soreness around your belly button or lower abdomen, you could have diastasis recti — which can happen when a growing belly causes abdominal muscles to separate and protrude slightly. Sometimes diastasis recti resolves on its own, but talk to your practitioner if it's not easing up. Most of the time the problem can be fixed with targeted core exercises.

In the meantime, think about all the incredible things your body has done over the last 40 weeks. And soak up this special time with your adorable newborn!

From before you begin to show to the time your baby finally arrives, your belly grows and changes in amazing ways. And now that you know more about your baby bump, you can appreciate everything it's doing even more. It's not only the warm, cozy home where your little one spends her first nine months, it's also one of your first ways to connect with each other before birth.

Pregnancy in 3 Words
